thread.title: Rotating Stocks To Grow Portfolio Earnings

author: Investment Pancake
title: Rotating Stocks To Grow Portfolio Earnings
text:
The goal of any well run company is to grow earnings per share over time without taking on too much incremental earnings risk. Why should managing a portfolio be any different from managing any other type of business?
To get the current earnings for my portfolio, I take a sum of the reported earnings per share for each company I own, multiplied by the number of shares I own. For the ETFs in my portfolio, I can pull the earnings data off the fund sponsor's home pages. For REITs, I use funds from operations ("FFO") instead of earnings, and for preferred stock funds, I use the yield as my calculation of earnings. With all that information, I can then track my portfolio's earnings growth by comparing this month's earnings with the portfolio's earnings this time last year.
Over time, my goal is to generate higher portfolio earnings growth than the overall earnings growth for the global stock market, and to do so at lower risk (which to my way of thinking means a lower PE ratio). According to Vanguard, the annual earnings growth for the Vanguard Total World Stock Index ETF ( VT ) clocks in at 8.4%, with a current PE ratio of 15.4 as of November 30th (which comes to about a PE ratio of 14.63 today).
As it happens, over the past year, the earnings growth for my portfolio comes in at 12.61%, with a current PE ratio of 14.88. My conclusion is that over this past year, I'm basically taking on slightly more risk than the overall market (since my portfolio PE ratio is slightly higher than the PE ratio for VT), and generating 4.21% in extra earnings growth.
That's fine, but I'd like to come up with a plan to boost my portfolio's earnings growth, lower my portfolio's overall PE ratio, or both. I can think of just three ways to do that.
Method one: reinvest more dividends into more shares, and thereby get more earnings. I'd love to do that, but I've already tapped out my supply of spare cash from last month's dividends.
Method two: invest in companies with higher earnings growth and lower PE ratios than the average earnings growth and PE ratio for VT. Well, I already do that. In addition, my investments are largely confined to companies with high credit ratings, healthy dividend yields, promising dividend growth, with high margin businesses enveloped in competitive advantages... all stewarded by capable managers who I'd happily hire if it were up to me.
Method three: sell companies I own that have very high PE ratios, and buy companies with lower PE ratios and that probably will have higher future earnings growth... all without compromising on the overall quality or by taking on additional credit risk.
It goes without saying that anyone who believes in efficient markets will conclude that methods two and three, listed above, are impossible. As it happens, the prevalence of that belief is precisely why I actively manage my portfolio. You see, it's not that I am convinced that I can continue to outperform the entire global stock market over long periods of time. No, my reason for actively managing my portfolio is because I'm pretty sure that passive investment can only work if relatively few people are doing it. Whenever someone tells you that you can earn money easily and without doing any work, they are probably lying to you, to themselves, or both. And no, I don't care if the person telling you that happens to have a Nobel prize in economics. Oh, and the idea that people who put in zero effort are virtually guaranteed to earn more money than people who put in lots of effort???? That studying your investments and looking for bargains is IRRATIONAL??? You gotta be kidding me! I mean, come on... do you really think that the stock market is going to just sort of benevolently take care of you like it was your fairy godmother, so you can just kick back and relax and freeload off all the other sucker investors who are wasting their time researching companies and looking for opportunities to buy earnings at a good price? I would have thought that the financial crisis of 2008 and 2009 would have beat that pie-eyed notion out of just about anyone, but fund flows into passive stock ETFs over the past decade prove otherwise. Any die hard efficient markets theorist would look at my portfolio and conclude that I've just been lucky over the last couple of decades, but as the late, great Samuel Goldwyn said, "the harder I work, the luckier I get."
Speaking of dumb luck, did you know that about seven or eight months ago, I bought shares of Church and Dwight ( CHD ) in one of my ROTH IRAs? It's a great company with an investment grade credit rating, that sells time-honored products imbued with brand loyalty, and impressive long-term growth in earnings per share.
The thing is, the stock trades at a stunning PE ratio of nearly 29. Wowzers.
I mean, I'm as happy with a 34% price gain in half a year, but honestly, do Trojan condoms and Arm and Hammer baking soda really warrant this sort of exuberant price behaviour? Let me be the first to assure you that I had zero idea whatsoever when I bought CHD that the price would go haywire, but when it comes to investing, it's not about guessing which stock pick is going to get lucky. It's about what you do with that luck that makes the difference. You'll see how in just a moment.
But first, we need to talk about the lugubrious case of Apple ( AAPL ). The long-term EPS growth is 27%, compared to the EPS growth rate of CHD which clocks in at 14% over the past decade. Not that the past is any guide to future performance, but when was the last time you saw lines wrapping around the block to buy baking soda and condoms? A few days ago, my wife literally couldn't physically enter the Apple store in Bethesda, Maryland on account of the crowds (although granted, Bethesda is a long way from China where the crowds at the Apple store have apparently thinned out of late).
And the PE ratio? It's 13. Now help me out here. Is CHD stock literally worth twice what AAPL stock is worth? I guess so, if you believe that the stock market is efficient, but frankly, the earnings numbers seem to be saying the exact opposite.
And and and... it gets even BETTER. Apple stock is going to crash when the market opens today, and when it does, that PE ratio is going to be even lower than it was yesterday.
So, if I sell a bit of CHD, I'll book a 34% gain completely free of income tax, and by purchasing Apple at a steep discount, I'll increase my portfolio earnings and, in my view, potential future earnings growth. All without sacrificing earnings quality (can anyone really say that Apple is more poorly managed than Church and Dwight?) or credit risk (Apple is no less capable of paying back its debts than Church and Dwight). Call me crazy, but I don't think the stock market is my benevolent fairy godmother. I think the stock market is a lying liar, and I'm happy to cash in on my random, lucky pick with now-overpriced shares of CHD, and park that capital where it's going to produce higher earnings for each of my investment dollars.
And I'm also bullish on Altria ( MO ), despite the fact that I think their recent investment in the legalized pot business was dramatically overpriced and that the company's credit rating is going to get cut as a result. 13 is the sort of PE ratio that just seems to be a theme for me today.
You know, I'm not a big fan of smoking pot, but it sure seems like there are plenty of people out there anxious to pay good money so they can get stoned. In the words of Old Him (AKA Bob Dylan); "evry body muzz git shtoned". Were it me, I'd switch the lyrics to "evry body muzz git dividends", but perhaps that's why I'm not winning any Nobel literature prizes anytime soon.
This chart is a thing of beauty and awe to value investors like me.
When I die, I hope to look down from heaven (or look up from that other place), and hear my close friends, beloved family members and acquaintances deliver my eulogy. "He sure was one cheap bastard."
I can't imagine a higher compliment. In fact, I'm going to spend the next six months not purchasing one single material item unless I literally cannot live without it. Why? I could tell you that it's because I'm tired of the consumer rat race, and mistaking what I want for what I need, but I won't lie to you. The real reason is because I'm a cheap bastard. I don't like to own expensive stocks any more than I like to own expensive shoes. In that sense, today's capital reallocation feels right and in keeping with my general outlook on life, and if I've learned one thing as an investor, it's that you should always be fundamentally comfortable with your approach in spite of whatever the stock market may or may not be doing on any given day or month.
Due to the time difference between Lisbon and the East Coast, I'll have to wait to write the conclusion of this article.
Several hours pass. I go to eat fish at the Campo Do Ourique Mercado. Drink a sake. Come back home and eagerly place my trades at precisely 2:32 pm local time.
So, what happened to my portfolio earnings when I sold CHD and bought AAPL and MO? Naturally they went up and now, my portfolio EPS growth rate has grown to 12.96% and the overall PE ratio for the portfolio has dropped to 14.83. My earnings performance relative to VT is a bit better, and I'm taking on a bit less risk than I was yesterday. Over the past year, my portfolio's price performance is 8.81% higher than the price performance of VT, but I'm chalking that up to noise since it exceeds my portfolio's relative earnings growth. After all, the stock market is a lying liar, and most certainly is not my fairy godmother.
